'''''A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits''''' is the title of a [[master's thesis]] written by [[computer science]] pioneer [[Claude Elwood Shannon|Claude E. Shannon]] while attending the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) in 1937,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Agarwal |first1=Ravi P |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bENTBQAAQBAJ&dq=claude+shannon+master%27s+thesis+1936&pg=PA425 |title=Creators of Mathematical and Computational Sciences |last2=Sen |first2=Syamal K |date=2014 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-319-10869-8 |location=Cham |pages=425 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-10870-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Fox |first=Charles |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aHO1EAAAQBAJ&dq=claude+shannon+worked+on+his+master%27s+thesis+in+1936&pg=PA114 |title=Computer Architecture: From the Stone Age to the Quantum Age |date=2024 |publisher=No Starch Press |isbn=978-1-7185-0286-4 |location=San Francisco |pages=114 |language=en}}</ref> and then published in 1938. In his thesis, Shannon, a dual degree graduate of the [[University of Michigan]], proved that [[Boolean algebra (logic)|Boolean algebra]]<ref>{{Cite book

  | last = Caldwell
  | first = Samuel H.
  | author-link = Samuel H. Caldwell
  | title = Switching Circuits and Logical Design, Sixth Printing
  | publisher = John Wiley & Sons
  | location = New York
  | year = 1965
  | orig-year = 1958
  | page = 34
  | isbn =  978-0471129691
  | quote = <!--He-->[Shannon] constructed a calculus based on a set of postulates which described basic switching ideas; e.g., an open circuit in series with an open circuit is an open circuit. Then he showed that his calculus was equivalent to certain elementary parts of the calculus of propositions, which in turn was derived from the algebra of logic developed by George Boole.
  }}</ref> could be used to simplify the arrangement of the [[relays]] that were the building blocks of the electromechanical [[automatic telephone exchange]]s of the day. He went on to prove that it should also be possible to use arrangements of relays to solve Boolean algebra problems. His thesis laid the foundations for all [[Computer#Digital computers|digital computing]] and [[Digital electronics|digital circuits]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wheen |first=Andrew |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B6shu_hAiGkC |title=Dot-Dash to Dot.Com: How Modern Telecommunications Evolved from the Telegraph to the Internet |date=2011 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-1-4419-6759-6 |location=New York, NY |pages=77 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-6760-2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Wright |first=Alex |author-link=Alex Wright |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Fd2gEAAAQBAJ |title=Informatica: Mastering Information through the Ages |date=2023 |publisher=Cornell University Press |isbn=978-1-5017-6867-5 |pages=188 |language=en |jstor=10.7591/j.ctv2rtgnvk }}</ref>

The utilization of the [[wikt:binary|binary]] properties of electrical switches to perform logic functions is the basic concept that underlies all [[digital computer|electronic digital computer]] designs. Shannon's thesis became the foundation of practical [[digital circuit]] design when it became widely known among the [[electrical engineering]] community during and after [[World War II]]. At the time, the methods employed to design logic circuits (for example, contemporary [[Konrad Zuse]]'s [[Z1 (computer)|Z1]]) were ''[[ad hoc]]'' in nature and lacked the theoretical discipline that Shannon's paper supplied to later projects.

Shannon's work also differed significantly in its approach and theoretical framework compared to the work of [[Akira Nakashima]]. Whereas Shannon's approach and framework was abstract and based on mathematics, Nakashima tried to extend the existent circuit theory of the time to deal with relay circuits, and was reluctant to accept the mathematical and abstract model, favoring a grounded approach.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Kawanishi |first=Toma |date=2019 |title=Prehistory of Switching Theory in Japan: Akira Nakashima and His Relay-circuit Theory |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/historiascientiarum/29/1/29_136/_article |journal=Historia Scientiarum |series=Second Series |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=136–162 |doi=10.34336/historiascientiarum.29.1_136}}</ref> Shannon's ideas broke new ground, with his abstract and modern approach dominating modern-day electrical engineering.<ref name=":0" />

The paper is commonly regarded as the most important master's thesis ever due to its insights and influence.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Norman |first=Jeremy M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=emmitTbOoFgC&dq=a+mathematical+theory+of+communication+the+most+important+paper&pg=PA749 |title=From Gutenberg to the Internet: A Sourcebook on the History of Information Technology |publisher=Historyofscience.com |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-930405-87-8 |location=Novato, Calif |pages=749 |language=en |oclc=ocm57124414}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Aleksander |first1=Igor |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j_S6CgAAQBAJ&dq=Aristotle%27s+Laptop:+The+Discovery+of+our+Informational+Mind+most+important+ms+thesis+ever&pg=PA22 |title=Aristotle's Laptop: The Discovery of our Informational Mind |last2=Morton |first2=Helen |date=2012 |publisher=[[World Scientific Publishing]] |isbn=978-981-4343-49-7 |series=Series on Machine Consciousness |volume=1 |pages=22 |language=en |doi=10.1142/8113}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Matthews |first1=Suzanne J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZX85EAAAQBAJ&dq=claude+shannon+masters+thesis+most+important+thesis&pg=PA234 |title=Dive Into Systems: A Gentle Introduction to Computer Systems |last2=Newhall |first2=Tia |last3=Webb |first3=Kevin C. |publisher=No Starch Press |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-7185-0136-2 |location=San Francisco |pages=234 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1737360314440786070 |user=pmddomingos |title=The most important master's thesis of all time. |first=Pedro |last=Domingos |author-link=Pedro Domingos |date=2023-12-20 |access-date=2024-11-05}}</ref> Pioneering computer scientist [[Herman Goldstine]] described Shannon's thesis as "surely{{nbsp}}... one of the most important master's theses ever written{{nbsp}}... It helped to change digital circuit design from an art to a science."{{refn|{{cite book|page=119-20|title=The Computer: From Pascal to von Neumann|last=Goldstine|first=Herman A.|year=1972}} }} In 1985, psychologist [[Howard Gardner]] called his thesis "possibly the most important, and also the most famous, master's thesis of the century".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Nancy Duvergne |date=2011-08-15 |title=Claude Shannon: Digital Pioneer's Work Still Reverberates |url=https://alum.mit.edu/slice/claude-shannon-digital-pioneers-work-still-reverberates |access-date=2024-01-11 |website=alum.mit.edu |language=en}}</ref> The paper won the [[Alfred Noble Prize#Recipients|1939 Alfred Noble Prize]].
